authority.scope: Supplemental evidence for the 92 questions that were bank-key-only before the Sutton–Barto pass
authority.book: Richard S. Sutton and Andrew G. Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction, second edition (2018), local PDF
authority.page_rule: printed_pages are the page numbers printed in the book; the local PDF page is printed page + 22
authority.coursera_rule: Only publicly visible official Coursera course descriptions and module/lesson titles were inspected; no gated lesson content was accessed.
authority.interpretation: canonical exam status is independent of evidence tier; all Q001–Q317 remain canonical

Q002.chapter_section: Ch. 8, §8.2 Dyna: Integrated Planning, Acting, and Learning
Q002.support: Dyna integrates direct learning, a learned model, and planning updates from simulated experience; its demonstrated benefit is learning faster from real interaction.
Q002.reference_answer: None of the options states the key benefit: improved sample efficiency through integrated planning and learning.

Q004.reason: The stem repurposes temporal-difference learning as flexible course scheduling; neither the RL textbook nor the official Alberta/Coursera pages use TD in that educational-delivery sense.

Q007.chapter_section: Ch. 2, §2.7 Upper-Confidence-Bound Action Selection; Ch. 8, §8.11 Monte Carlo Tree Search
Q007.support: MCTS may use UCB as its tree policy, and the positive UCB constant controls the degree of exploration, so increasing it favors uncertainty more strongly.

Q010.support: Tile coding provides sparse, computationally efficient features and generalization across nearby states; memory efficiency depends on the lookup-table comparison and implementation.

Q015.reason: Classical policy iteration is developed for a fixed MDP; the public Coursera page lists 'Flexibility of the Policy Iteration Framework' but does not publicly explain adaptation to changed dynamics or goals.

Q019.chapter_section: Ch. 10, §§10.3 and 10.5 Average Reward and Differential Semi-gradient Sarsa
Q019.support: Differential values are defined through expectations, average reward, and Bellman-style equations; no single listed branch of mathematics is uniquely essential.

Q028.chapter_section: Ch. 5, §5.5 Off-policy Prediction via Importance Sampling
Q028.support: Importance-sampling variance depends on likelihood ratios and the relationship between target and behavior distributions; complexity alone does not determine variance.
Q028.reference_answer: No fixed effect follows from making a proposal distribution more complex; closeness and coverage relative to the target matter.

Q033.support: UCB is a valid MCTS tree policy, and its exploration constant controls how strongly uncertain actions are favored.

Q035.reason: The book links overfitting to approximator capacity, limited data, and validation performance, but does not rank the four named RL algorithm families by inherent overfitting risk.

Q037.support: DQN stores transition tuples in replay memory and repeatedly samples past experiences for Q-learning updates, reducing correlation and instability.
Q037.reference_answer: B — storing and reusing past experiences to stabilize learning.

Q038.chapter_section: Ch. 9, §9.7 Nonlinear Function Approximation: Artificial Neural Networks
Q038.support: The book recommends monitoring performance on validation data distinct from training data to detect generalization failure and overfitting.
Q038.reference_answer: B — validate the model on new/held-out data.

Q039.reason: The textbook treats Monte Carlo returns and estimates, not the generic simulation-output claim in the options; the allowed Coursera pages do not resolve it.

Q042.reason: Sutton–Barto shows sampled gradients in reinforcement learning, but it does not compare the listed application fields or disprove the supplied computer-graphics option.

Q043.reason: The stem uses temporal difference as an educational delivery model; the allowed sources use it only as an RL prediction/control method.

Q047.support: Average reward is estimated incrementally inside differential TD/control algorithms such as differential semi-gradient Sarsa.
Q047.reference_answer: A differential average-reward TD/control method; D is directionally right but too broad.

Q048.support: Backpropagation is widely used to train neural function approximators in RL, including DQN, so it is not a method 'not typically used' in RL.
Q048.reference_answer: None of the options: Q-learning, Sarsa, DDPG, and backpropagation are all used in RL, though backpropagation is an optimizer rather than an RL algorithm.

Q053.reason: The public course page covers epsilon-greedy exploration, but neither it nor the cited book passage establishes a particular decaying-epsilon schedule as asked.

Q054.support: TD(0) prediction evaluates a fixed policy and has no exploration choice; exploration enters control algorithms such as Sarsa through the behavior policy.
Q054.reference_answer: No exploration–exploitation parameter belongs to TD(0) prediction; in TD control, an exploration parameter such as epsilon controls it.

Q056.support: The book names gradual reward-guided successive training as shaping, a term absent from the options.

Q060.reason: The stem treats TD as a self-paced learning format rather than temporal-difference RL; the allowed sources cannot answer it.

Q064.support: Optimistic bias is reduced as action-value estimates are repeatedly updated; a decaying exploration rate does not directly remove the initial optimism.
Q064.reference_answer: Repeated value updates wash out the optimistic estimates; none of the options states this mechanism.

Q066.support: Policy-gradient methods directly parameterize and optimize a policy, whereas DQN combines Q-learning with a deep action-value network.
Q066.reference_answer: A — DQN is value-based, not a policy-gradient variation.

Q069.support: Shaping can address sparse reward by guiding the learner through easier stages, but it is not simply or universally 'encouraging less obvious actions'.
Q069.reference_answer: Reward shaping supplies informative intermediate guidance when rewards are sparse; B is only a loose possible effect.

Q070.reason: The book defines a softmax distribution but does not introduce a temperature parameter, and the public Coursera page exposes only the lesson title, not its mechanics.

Q074.support: Expected Sarsa explicitly sums action values over the policy and is computationally more complex than Sarsa, so large action spaces do not provide the claimed preference.
Q074.reference_answer: The premise is false without extra structure; Expected Sarsa can be more expensive because it computes an expectation over actions.

Q078.chapter_section: Ch. 5, §5.4 Monte Carlo Control without Exploring Starts
Q078.support: An epsilon-soft policy assigns every action at least epsilon divided by the action count; flexibility, transparency, rigidity, and accountability are not its defining characteristics.
Q078.reference_answer: No unique option; use the probability-floor definition of epsilon-soft.

Q080.support: The book states that, ignoring technical details, worst-case DP time for a finite MDP is polynomial in the numbers of states and actions.

Q083.reason: The accessibility claim concerns online education, not temporal-difference reinforcement learning.

Q085.support: The UCB bonus explicitly depends on how often an action has been selected and favors uncertain/under-sampled actions.

Q089.reason: This is a star-exploration engineering item outside the permitted RL references.

Q091.support: Policy-gradient updates include a step-size/learning-rate parameter, so it affects training behavior, but discounting, sampling variance, and regularization can also affect stability.
Q091.reference_answer: A is a valid factor, not a uniquely exhaustive one.

Q092.reason: The real-time feedback/interactivity claim is about pedagogy and is not a claim about temporal-difference RL in either allowed reference.

Q094.support: The UCB exploration bonus depends on both a parent/overall visit count and the candidate action's visit count; MCTS may use that rule as its tree policy.
Q094.reference_answer: Both parent-node visits and child/action visits, commonly through sqrt(log N(parent)/N(parent,action)); D is incomplete.

Q095.reason: The allowed public materials identify epsilon-greedy exploration but do not publicly state the decaying-epsilon schedule asked here.

Q099.support: The book explicitly names UCB as a tree-policy rule that balances exploration and exploitation in MCTS.

Q101.support: The MCTS UCB term uses both the total/parent visit count and the action-specific visit count, not merely one count.
Q101.reference_answer: Both parent and action visit counts; D is incomplete.

Q102.support: Broad features enable transfer/generalization between similar states while sufficient feature resolution preserves fine discrimination.
Q102.reference_answer: C — apply knowledge to similar situations while retaining distinctions.

Q109.support: Dyna unifies direct RL, model learning, planning, and acting; it is not primarily a general architecture for modeling complex dynamic systems.
Q109.reference_answer: None of the options: Dyna integrates learning, a model, simulated planning updates, and acting.

Q111.reason: The stem describes educational feedback, not the TD error/update mechanism in reinforcement learning.

Q112.support: The agent's objective is to maximize total reward over the long run, which matches the cumulative-reward part of option B.
Q112.reference_answer: B — learn a policy/strategy that maximizes expected cumulative reward.

Q115.chapter_section: Ch. 5, §5.5 Off-policy Prediction via Importance Sampling
Q115.support: Ordinary importance sampling can have unbounded or infinite variance, while weighted or carefully designed variants can reduce it.
Q115.reference_answer: Importance sampling is variance-reducing only with an appropriate proposal/estimator; weighted IS is lower variance than ordinary IS in the book's setting.

Q117.reason: Hyperbolic discounting is not treated in the textbook or the public Alberta/Coursera course descriptions.

Q125.reason: This is a generic task-management claim; episodic RL definitions do not establish flexibility as the crucial management factor.

Q134.support: MCTS maintains exploration through its rollout/tree policies such as UCB or randomized playouts; reducing rollouts reduces evidence rather than maintaining exploration.
Q134.reference_answer: C — reducing the number of rollouts.

Q136.chapter_section: Ch. 2, §2.10 Summary discussion of Bayesian bandits
Q136.support: The book defines posterior/Thompson sampling as selecting actions according to their posterior probability of being best.

Q139.support: Function approximation is used when state spaces exceed available memory, and DQN uses a neural network to approximate optimal action values.
Q139.reference_answer: A — DQN, if 'optimal value' means the optimal action-value function.

Q144.support: Episodic versus continuing is determined by a terminal boundary, not by how frequently an activity occurs; exam preparation can be episodic if the exam is the terminal boundary.
Q144.reference_answer: A only under the natural formulation where the preparation episode terminates at the exam; otherwise the task description is underspecified.

Q145.support: Dyna uses an environment model of transition/reward dynamics, but its defining concern is integrating that model with planning, learning, and acting.
Q145.reference_answer: B can mean a model of environment dynamics, but 'dynamic models' is not the book's defining category.

Q148.reason: The behavioral-stimulus discrimination example is not defined by the permitted RL references.

Q151.support: A distribution model supplies all next-state/reward possibilities and probabilities for expected updates; the book does not claim broader-scenario generalization as its key advantage.
Q151.reference_answer: Its distinguishing advantage is enabling expected updates from a full transition/reward distribution; none of the options states this precisely.

Q152.support: Sample updates are cheaper but noisier, while expected updates use more computation; the book gives no universal sample-efficiency ordering between sample and distribution models.
Q152.reference_answer: No universal ordering; the trade-off depends on model acquisition, computation, branching, and accuracy.

Q154.support: Lower lambda shortens traces and moves the method toward one-step TD/more bootstrapping; the book does not state that it universally causes one listed failure.
Q154.reference_answer: Lower lambda makes the update more TD-like and can increase bootstrap bias, but 'updates become more biased' is not an unconditional theorem.

Q163.reason: The book covers function-approximation generalization, not the behavioral stimulus-response definition used by this item.

Q224.support: Both Monte Carlo and temporal-difference methods estimate action values without an environment model.

Q238.support: The step size multiplies the newest reward's estimation error and therefore controls how much the latest observation changes the estimate.
Q238.reference_answer: B — the influence of the most recent reward on the estimate.

Q240.support: Nonlinear parameterized approximators generally may reach only local optima, so local optima are a real challenge, though not a universally unique 'main' challenge.

Q252.support: Off-policy learning uses data generated by a behavior policy to learn about a different target policy; it still learns from actions actually taken.
Q252.reference_answer: Behavior and target policies differ; none of the options says this correctly.

Q257.reference_answer: None of the options states Dyna's actual purpose.

Q270.reason: Time-blocking is a productivity technique, not an episodic-RL method established by the permitted references.

Q294.chapter_section: Ch. 13, §13.7 Policy Parameterization for Continuous Actions
Q294.support: Gaussian policy parameters are directly updated by policy-gradient methods and can be used in actor–critic; Q-learning is not the policy-parameter learning method presented.

Q303.support: DP, Monte Carlo, and TD are solution/learning method families for MDPs, whereas stochastic gradient descent is an optimizer used inside some approximate methods.
Q303.reference_answer: D at the intended algorithm-family level.

Q307.reason: Hyperbolic versus exponential human time preference is not covered by the allowed sources, so the supplied directional comparison cannot be adjudicated from them.

Q311.support: Policy evaluation seeks the value function satisfying the Bellman equation and uses it as an update/consistency relation; the equation is not an objective function.
Q311.reference_answer: No listed objective is precise; policy evaluation computes v_pi, commonly as the fixed point of the Bellman expectation equation.

Q314.support: Softmax selects actions from a probability distribution derived from learned action preferences, though the book distinguishes preferences from value estimates.
Q314.reference_answer: C — softmax, with the caveat that its inputs may be preferences rather than estimated value functions.
